readerTitle: Your competitor might not be in your industry
caseNote: 실제 기업 (FedEx의 ZapMail, 1984~1986) + 가상 적용 (서류 배송 업체, 번역 회사)
insight: 경쟁자는 같은 상품을 파는 회사가 아니라, 고객이 같은 일을 해결하려고 고를 수 있는 모든 방법이다.
misconception: 우리 경쟁자는 같은 업종에서 같은 상품을 파는 회사들뿐이다.

sources.text: Porter, M. (1979). How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy. Harvard Business Review. (대체재의 위협)
FedEx ZapMail 출시(1984)와 중단(1986)에 관한 당시 언론 보도 및 FedEx 회사 연혁 자료

factChecks.note: ZapMail 출시 연도(1984)와 중단 연도(1986)를 FedEx 연혁 또는 당시 보도(예: New York Times 1986년 기사)로 확인하세요.
ZapMail 손실 규모는 보도마다 다릅니다(약 3억~3억 5천만 달러로 알려짐). 카드에는 "hundreds of millions of dollars"로만 적었습니다.
ZapMail의 작동 방식(FedEx 지점 간 팩스 전송 후 쿠리어가 몇 시간 안에 배달)과, 사무실용 팩스 기계 가격 하락이 실패 원인으로 꼽힌다는 점을 확인하세요. 기술 문제(위성 계획 등)도 함께 거론되므로 카드에는 "one big reason"으로 적었습니다.
이후 FedEx 사업이 소포 중심으로 성장했다는 서술은 일반적 설명입니다. 구체 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your competitor might not be in your industry
body: In the 1980s, FedEx was winning the overnight delivery race against other couriers.
Its most dangerous rival wasn't another delivery company. It was a beige box sitting on office desks.

image.label: Competitors are other ways to get the same job done.
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 큰 배송 트럭, 오른쪽 책상 위에 작은 1980년대 팩스 기계. 팩스에서 종이 한 장이 나오고, 트럭은 그 종이를 바라보는 듯한 구도. 실제 회사 로고나 색상 도장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What threatens your prices most?
body: You run a courier firm that rushes signed contracts between law offices across the city. You're faster and cheaper than the other two couriers in town.
Over the next five years, which threat should worry you most?

options.text: A new courier opening with lower prices
options.feedback: A real risk, but a rival courier still has to pay for riders and vans. It can only undercut you so far.

options.text: Law offices sending signed documents electronically
options.feedback: This removes the trip entirely. It doesn't compete on your terms, so being the best courier won't protect you.
It squeezes your margins, but it squeezes every courier. Customers still need a courier, so you can pass some of it on.

cards.title: FedEx tried to own the fax. The fax won anyway.
body: In 1984, FedEx launched **ZapMail**. Customers handed a document to FedEx, which faxed it between its own offices and had a courier deliver the copy within hours.
But fax machines kept getting cheaper. Businesses bought their own and sent pages in seconds, with no courier and no fee. One big reason ZapMail failed: customers could do the job themselves.
FedEx shut ZapMail down in 1986, after losses reported in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

cards.title: Substitutes
body: A **substitute** is a product from a different industry that does the same job for the customer.
The customer's job wasn't "ship an envelope." It was "get this page to Chicago today." A courier, a fax and later email all do that job. They just do it in completely different ways.
Industry lists show you rivals. Asking about the customer's job shows you substitutes.

image.label: One job in the center, three different ways to do it around it
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 말풍선 "Get this page to Chicago today". 주변에 세 갈래 화살표로 "Courier", "Fax", "Email" 아이콘. 같은 목적지로 모이는 구도. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Substitutes put a ceiling on your price.
body: Even with no rival couriers at all, a courier can't charge much more than a fax costs. Past that point, customers switch ways of doing the job, not suppliers.
list: **The ceiling:** your price can't rise far above the substitute's total cost to the customer
**The squeeze:** each time the substitute gets cheaper or better, the ceiling drops
**The blind spot:** it rarely shows up in your industry's reports
cards.callout: The threat grows with value for money, not with how many rivals you can name.

cards.title: Look for the other ways to get the job done.
body: A business-travel agency competes with video calls. A steel maker competes with aluminium and plastic for car parts. A café near offices competes with the free coffee machine upstairs.
In each case, the substitute comes from outside the industry, and it sets limits on what the industry can charge.
cards.softwareNote: For many business software products, the strongest substitute isn't another app. It's a spreadsheet plus email. If your price feels high next to "we'll just use a shared sheet," that's your real ceiling.

cards.title: Not every new option is a threat.
body: Substitutes often start worse. Early faxes were blurry. That's why they get ignored. Watch the trend in price and quality, and how easy it is for customers to switch.
But don't panic over everything new. Some substitutes stall, and some only take part of your market. FedEx survived because its main business moved toward packages, something a fax can't send.

cards.title: Now it's a translation agency.
body: Your agency translates contracts and manuals for manufacturers. Clients now run drafts through free machine translation tools. The results are rough but improving fast.

options.feedback: You'd lose margin racing toward a price of nearly zero. A cheaper agency still costs more than a free tool.

options.text: Use the tools yourself, and sell expert review where errors are costly
options.feedback: You stop fighting the substitute on its strength and charge for what it can't promise: accuracy on legal and safety text. You may serve fewer clients at first.

options.text: Launch your own machine translation portal and charge per word
options.feedback: It shows you see the threat, but like ZapMail, you'd charge for a job customers can already do themselves for free.

cards.title: Your competitor is anything that does your customer's job.
body: Define the job, not the product. Then look outside your industry for other ways to get it done. They set your price ceiling.
**Try it today:** write down the job your customers hire you for. List three ways they could get it done without any business like yours.
